pillar.label: PILLAR ARTICLE · HOMEOWNER GUIDE
pillar.title: Who Works For You
intro: When a storm hits your home in {{CITY}}, your insurance company opens a file and puts a team of professionals to work right away. Most homeowners assume the person who shows up with a ladder is there to make sure they get paid fairly, but that person works for the carrier, and you have the legal right to bring in your own licensed representative. Do you know who is actually looking out for your side of the claim before you sign anything?

Filing a claim feels like a simple paperwork process until the first repair estimate comes back way lower than what a local contractor charges. You want to trust that your policy will cover the damage you paid premiums to protect, but insurance contracts are written in dense language that makes it easy to miss money you are owed unless someone reads every page for you. Have you had a chance to look at your policy's actual replacement rules, or would you like me to walk through them with you?
pillar.quote: Your insurance company has a full team protecting their bottom line, and you deserve someone protecting yours.
pillar.lead: The moment you call in a loss and get a claim number, your insurance company puts four different layers of people on your file. You only ever see one of them in person, but knowing how the other three operate behind the scenes helps you understand why claims get delayed or underpaid. Would you like to know what happens to your file after the inspection truck leaves your driveway?
team: They are often an independent contractor hired for the day who may work for several different insurance companies at once. They are usually friendly and polite while measuring and taking photos, but they do not have the authority to decide what you get paid. Have you already had someone walk your property, or are you still waiting for that first visit?

They read your claim notes first, tell the field adjuster what to look at, often just the roof, so nobody checks your ceilings or walls, and review the final report line by line. But you can submit your own complete proof of all interior and exterior damage so nothing gets left off the table. Did the person who inspected your home check inside your attic and ceilings?

The manager who watches the claim numbers and keeps total payouts in line. A desk adjuster's authority can stop at a certain dollar limit, but a documented, line-by-line estimate backed by your policy language can push your claim to a proper review. Are you worried your claim is stuck waiting on someone higher up?

As long as a homeowner accepts the first check and nobody pushes back on a low estimate or a partial denial, the lawyers never have to get involved. But you do not have to accept an unfair settlement just to avoid a fight when a licensed advocate can negotiate the numbers for you.
pillar.close_h: Four people work for your insurance company. Who works for you?
pillar.close: That's my job. I work only for you. I inspect the whole house, inside and out, build my own estimate, and handle the back-and-forth with your insurance company. Are you ready to talk about getting someone in your corner?
pillar.why: I became a licensed public adjuster in {{LICENSED_SINCE}} because I saw too many good families in {{CITY}} accept low payouts simply because they did not know how the claim system works. Insurance policies are complicated, but when someone explains your rights in plain English and documents every inch of damage, the playing field evens out. Ready to tell me what happened to your home?
steps: We talk about what happened to your home, look at your policy and any letters you already got from the insurer, and I give you an honest look at where your claim stands, at no cost.
I come out to your home, inspect the roof, walls, ceilings and hidden areas, and document every bit of damage the carrier may have missed.
I put together a detailed repair estimate and handle the calls, emails and paperwork with your insurance company so you don't have to.

faq: Why is my first insurance check way smaller than my roofer's estimate?

Insurance companies usually pay claims in two parts, starting with the depreciated value of your damaged property rather than the full replacement cost. They can also leave out local building code upgrades, labor rates, or hidden water damage that a contractor sees right away. But you may be able to recover the held-back money and add missed items once the full scope of repairs is properly documented and submitted.
I review your insurer's payout sheet side by side with real local repair costs to find what they left out.
Want to send over your insurance estimate so we can see why the numbers are so far apart?
The adjuster only spent ten minutes on my roof and never came inside. Is that normal?

Field adjusters often carry heavy caseloads after a Florida storm and may only have instructions from the desk adjuster to look at one specific area. When they rush through a roof check and skip the attic or ceilings, water intrusion and lifted shingles easily go unrecorded. But an incomplete inspection does not close the door on your claim when you bring in thorough photo and moisture documentation.
I walk your whole home, inside and out, and document what the first inspection missed.
Would you like me to come out and do a full top-to-bottom check?
Should I cash the first check the insurance company sent me?

Many homeowners freeze when a check arrives because they worry that depositing it means the claim is finished forever. In many cases, cashing an initial undisputed payment does not stop you from asking for the rest of what you are owed, but always check the memo line and the letter that came with it to make sure it does not say "full and final settlement."
I look at the paperwork that came with your check before you endorse it, so you know what rights you keep.
Did a letter come with that check, and would you like me to look it over with you?
My claim was denied for "wear and tear." Can I still fight it?

Insurers frequently blame roof leaks and missing shingles on old age or normal wear and tear, especially on Florida roofs over ten years old. A denial letter feels like the final word, but storm wind and hail leave damage patterns that differ from simple aging when documented correctly.
I inspect denied roofs for storm damage and build a factual response for your carrier.
When did you get your denial letter, and can we talk about what the roof actually looks like?
How much does it cost to hire a public adjuster in Florida?

Public adjusters usually work on a contingency fee, which means you pay nothing upfront and pay a percentage of the claim money recovered. Fees vary by claim and by whether the state has declared an emergency, but Florida law caps what we can charge and requires that you get the fee in writing before signing any contract.
I go over my written fee agreement line by line with you first so there are no surprises.
Would you like to talk through how the fee works on a claim like yours before you decide?
Will my insurance company drop me or raise my rates if I hire a public adjuster?

Florida homeowners worry about losing coverage in a tough insurance market, and carriers do adjust rates after major storms. Rate and renewal decisions depend on your insurer and your policy, but hiring a licensed public adjuster is your right, and your agent can tell you how a claim affects your policy.
I handle the claim professionally and keep your repair timeline on track.
Are you holding back on getting help because you're worried how your carrier will react?
Should I make repairs before the insurance adjuster comes to look at my house?

You have a duty under your policy to protect your home from further damage, like tarping a leaking roof or extracting standing water. Tearing out drywall or replacing a roof before the insurer sees it can hurt your claim, but clear photos and videos taken before emergency dry-out protect both your house and your claim.
I tell you what temporary steps to take right now and how to document everything before permanent work starts.
Have you already started emergency repairs, or are you figuring out what to do first?
What is "recoverable depreciation" and how do I get it back?

When an insurer calculates your loss, it subtracts a percentage for the age and condition of your roof or flooring and holds that money back until the work is done. That held-back amount is called recoverable depreciation, but if you have a Replacement Cost Value policy, you can claim it once you show proof that repairs are underway or done.
I track your depreciation holdbacks and submit the right invoices so the carrier releases the rest.
Do you see a depreciation line on your claim summary that hasn't been paid yet?
Can't my roofer or general contractor just handle the insurance claim for me?

Good contractors know how to rebuild your house and can give you a fair price for their trade. Under Florida law, a contractor cannot negotiate your insurance settlement unless they also hold a public adjuster license, but working alongside a public adjuster lets your contractor focus on building while I handle the policy and pricing.
I coordinate directly with your contractor so the approved scope matches what it takes to fix your home.
Has a contractor already given you a quote your insurance company is pushing back on?
How long do I have to file or reopen a storm claim in Florida?

Florida has strict deadlines for reporting a new claim and shorter windows for a supplemental claim when hidden damage shows up later. Waiting too long can bar you from collecting money you are owed, but acting quickly preserves your right to reopen an underpaid file.
I check your date of loss against current Florida deadlines right away.
When did the damage happen, and would you like to check how much time you have left?

articles.title: Why Is My First Insurance Check Smaller Than My Estimate?
articles.captures: Why is my insurance payout so low compared to my contractor estimate?
articles.short: Your first insurance check is usually smaller because the carrier subtracts depreciation for the age of your home and can leave out hidden repairs or local code upgrades. Under a replacement cost policy, this first check is rarely the final amount owed, but you have to document the missing items and request the rest properly. Have you looked at the line-by-line breakdown that came with your payment yet?
body: Opening an envelope from your insurance company and seeing a check for half of what your contractor quoted is a sinking feeling. Most homeowners assume the insurer simply refused to pay for their roof or interior repairs, but the gap usually comes down to how insurance math works and what the first inspector left off the list. Would you like to know the reasons that check came up short?

The biggest reason is called depreciation, which is how insurers reduce the value of your shingles, drywall or flooring based on how old they are. If your roof is twelve years old, the company may hold back thousands of dollars from the first check until you prove the repairs are being made, but if you have a Replacement Cost Value policy, that held-back money still belongs to you once the proper paperwork is filed. Do you know whether your policy pays Replacement Cost or Actual Cash Value?

The second reason is that the first scope of work often misses real construction steps. An estimate may only pay to replace a small patch of shingles or paint one wall, ignoring that brittle shingles break when lifted or paint won't match across an open room, but showing why a partial repair won't work makes the carrier look at the full repair area. Did your insurer's estimate only pay to patch a small section?

The third reason is hidden damage that nobody looked for during a quick walkthrough. Water travels behind baseboards, under laminate flooring and through attic insulation long before a brown stain shows on your ceiling, but a thorough moisture check and full inspection can bring those unseen repairs into your claim. Has anyone checked behind your walls or inside your attic since the storm?

Many people also forget the hurricane or all-peril deductible when they look at the bottom line. In Florida, hurricane deductibles are often two to five percent of your home's insured value, which takes a big bite out of the first payout, but when the total damage is undercounted, your deductible can eat almost the whole check. Is your deductible taking up most of the money they sent you?

Finally, estimating software can use pricing that doesn't reflect what licensed tradespeople in {{CITY}} actually charge after a major storm. Labor and material costs jump when everyone in town needs a roof at the same time, but accurate local repair bids and code requirements help bring the numbers closer to reality. Have you compared the prices on your insurance sheet against a real local bid?
articles.quote: The first check is an opening offer based on a quick look, not the final word on your home.
next: Print the full Statement of Loss and repair estimate, not just the cover letter with the check.
Ask a licensed local contractor for a detailed, room-by-room estimate to compare against the insurer's list.
Find the column labeled "Depreciation" to see how much money is being held back.
Photograph any cracked tiles, lifted shingles or interior water spots that aren't on the adjuster's report.
Call a licensed public adjuster to review both estimates side by side before you sign repair contracts.
articles.close: You should not have to drain your savings to cover repairs your insurance policy was supposed to pay for. Many homeowners accept the first check and move on without asking questions, but a careful review of your estimate can uncover repairs and held-back funds that were left out. Want to call or text me, {{FIRST}}, at {{PHONE}} so we can go over your payout sheet together?

articles.title: Should I Cash My Insurance Check If It Is Too Low?
articles.captures: Should I cash the first check from my insurance company?
articles.short: In many cases, cashing a first check for undisputed damages does not stop you from asking for the rest of your claim money. Read the check and any letter with it first to make sure it doesn't say "full and final settlement," but a second set of eyes on the paperwork protects your right to supplement the claim. Have you already deposited the check, or is it still sitting on your kitchen counter?
body: When a check shows up for a fraction of your repair bill, it's smart to pause before walking into the bank. Homeowners hear stories about people signing away their rights by endorsing a low settlement check, but knowing what to look for removes the guesswork so you can get repairs started safely. Would you like to know which words on a check should make you stop?

Insurance companies generally pay the undisputed amount they agree they owe. Cashing that check gives you money to tarp, dry out or order materials while the rest of the claim is negotiated, but if the memo line or letter says cashing it settles the entire claim, depositing it can lock you out of future payments. Have you checked the front and back of the check for release language?

Another wrinkle comes when you still have a mortgage on your home in {{CITY}}. Your mortgage company's name will almost always be on the check next to yours, so you can't cash it without their endorsement, but knowing their inspection and draw rules ahead of time keeps your money from getting stuck in red tape. Is your mortgage lender listed on the check?

Some homeowners hold onto a low check for months, thinking it sends a message. Leaving a check in a drawer doesn't make the carrier raise its offer, and checks can expire after ninety or one hundred eighty days, but depositing an undisputed payment while telling the carrier in writing that you dispute the balance keeps your money working for you. Are you worried that cashing it tells the insurer you agree with their number?

If your check came without a detailed breakdown, don't rush to spend it before seeing the math. You have the right to see every room, measurement and price the desk adjuster used, but once you have the full estimate, you can deposit the undisputed portion and submit a supplemental claim for everything they missed. Did the insurance company send you the full line-by-line estimate?
articles.quote: Cashing an undisputed check starts your recovery. Signing a final release ends your claim.
next: Read the memo line, the back of the check, and every page of the letter in the envelope.
Look for phrases like "full and final payment," "release of all claims" or "accord and satisfaction" before signing.
Keep the check stub and take a clear photo of the check for your claim folder.
If your mortgage company is on the check, call its loss draft department to learn the endorsement steps.
Have a licensed public adjuster review the Statement of Loss so you can file a supplement for the unpaid balance.
articles.close: A small first check doesn't mean your claim is over, as long as you handle the paperwork carefully from day one. Insurance companies issue partial payments every day, and many homeowners are too nervous or confused to ask for the rest, but you can use that first check to protect your home while I work for the full amount owed under your policy. Ready to call or text {{FIRST}} at {{PHONE}} so we can check that letter together before you go to the bank?

articles.title: What To Do When the Adjuster Only Looked at My Roof
articles.captures: The insurance adjuster only checked my roof and ignored the inside damage. What do I do?
articles.short: When an adjuster only inspects your roof and skips the inside of your home, your estimate can miss hidden water damage, wet insulation and stained ceilings. Field adjusters often follow narrow instructions from a desk adjuster, but you can request a re-inspection and submit full interior documentation to get every damaged room included. Did the adjuster who visited ever ask to step inside?
body: It happens after almost every windstorm in {{CITY}}: a ladder goes up, someone walks the shingles for ten minutes, and they drive away without knocking on your front door. Homeowners feel brushed off when an inspector ignores the inside of the house, but understanding why they skip the interior shows you how to get those rooms added to your claim. Would you like to know why the field adjuster stayed outside?

Many field adjusters are independent contractors given instructions from the desk adjuster before they arrive. If your first phone report only mentioned roof damage, the inspection may have been set up for the roof only, but wind-driven rain and lifted shingles often push water into your attic and down into your drywall. Have you noticed musty smells, bubbled paint or faint yellow rings on your ceilings since the storm?

Even when water hasn't soaked through to your living room ceiling yet, wet attic insulation and roof decking cause serious problems in Florida's heat and humidity. Wet insulation trapped above your drywall invites mold and wood rot, but documenting moisture in the attic shows the storm damage goes deeper than a few missing shingles. Has anyone climbed into your attic with a flashlight since the storm?

Water also travels sideways along rafters and wires, so a leak over the garage can show up as warped flooring or swollen baseboards two rooms away. A ten-minute roof walk will never connect those dots, but a complete room-by-room inspection ties your interior damage back to the storm opening on your roof. Are you seeing water spots or warped trim in rooms that aren't right under the roof damage?

If you already got an estimate that only lists roof items, your claim file is incomplete. Insurance companies won't pay to paint ceilings, replace wet insulation or dry out drywall unless someone puts those measurements and photos in front of the desk adjuster, but a complete interior and exterior scope gives them what they need to reopen the file and account for the whole house. Would you like help documenting the inside of your home before the damage gets worse?
articles.quote: A storm rarely stops at the shingles, and your inspection shouldn't stop there either.
next: Walk through every room in daylight and look closely at ceilings, crown molding, window frames and closets.
Take clear, well-lit photos and videos of every stain, crack or swollen baseboard you find.
If it's safe, check your attic hatch for damp insulation or dark water trails on the rafters.
Write down the date you first noticed each spot so your file has a clear timeline.
Call a licensed public adjuster for a full top-to-bottom inspection.
articles.close: You pay for coverage on your entire home, not just the shingles on top of it. Letting an incomplete inspection stand can leave you paying out of pocket for drywall, paint and insulation months from now, but a thorough interior inspection puts the full truth of your loss on the record. Want to call or text {{FIRST}} at {{PHONE}} to schedule a complete walkthrough of your home?

articles.title: My Roof Claim Was Denied for Wear and Tear. Now What?
articles.captures: How do I fight a homeowners insurance denial for wear and tear?
articles.short: A denial letter blaming "wear and tear" is one of the most common responses Florida homeowners get, especially on roofs over ten years old. Insurance companies sometimes blame age when wind damage is subtle, but a denial letter is not the final word if a proper inspection shows a recent storm damaged your roof. Did your denial letter say your roof simply died of old age?
body: Getting a denial letter after years of paying premiums on time feels like a slap in the face. The letter usually quotes policy exclusions and says your leaks or missing shingles are normal aging, but subtle wind creases and lifted seals can be mistaken for ordinary wear and tear. Would you like to know the difference between an old roof and a storm-damaged roof?

Every roof in {{CITY}} takes a beating from the Florida sun, and older shingles lose granules over time. High winds leave specific damage: shingles lift, bend back, crease across the top and lose their seal so rain blows underneath, but a quick look from the ground or a rushed photo report can miss broken seals until someone checks the shingles by hand. Did the adjuster actually check whether your shingles were unsealed or creased?

Another reason insurers deny older roofs is that brittle shingles crack when a roofer lifts them to slide in a replacement. When a repair attempt breaks the surrounding shingles, building rules can require replacing more than a patch, but carriers sometimes call that brittleness wear and tear. Has a local roofer told you your roof is too brittle to patch?

Many homeowners put the denial letter in a drawer and start looking at loans to pay for a new roof themselves. Walking away without a second opinion means paying for it all yourself, but having a licensed public adjuster re-inspect the roof and respond with clear photo evidence can give the carrier a reason to take a second look. Are you about to pay out of pocket just because the first letter said no?

Time matters once you get a denial, because your roof is still exposed to the next afternoon storm and Florida sets deadlines for disputing a claim decision. Leaving damaged shingles alone can lead to new leaks the insurer may blame on neglect, but acting quickly lets you protect your home and dispute the decision while the storm evidence is still fresh. When did you get your denial letter, and have you kept the water out since?
articles.quote: An old roof can still be damaged by a storm, and a denial letter is not the final word.
next: Save the denial letter and its envelope, and write down the date you received it.
Ask your insurance company for the field adjuster's photos and inspection report.
Tarp any active leaks right away and keep the receipt for the tarp and labor.
Don't let anyone tear off the roof before you get a second inspection.
Have a licensed public adjuster inspect the roof for wind creases, unsealed tabs and storm patterns.
articles.close: Many homeowners give up the moment they read a denial letter. You don't have to take one adjuster's opinion as the final truth when your own eyes tell you the roof was fine before the storm hit {{CITY}}, but you need clear, documented proof to make the carrier take a second look. Ready to call or text {{FIRST}} at {{PHONE}} so we can review your denial letter and look at your roof together?
